question.worked_solution:
First, we apply the sum and constant factor rules and take the coefficients out of the integral. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{10}{x}-\sqrt[3]{x})\text{d}x & =10\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x-\int {x}^{1/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{{x}^{1/3+1}}{(\frac{1}{3}+1)}+C \\  & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{3}{4}{x}^{4/3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=10\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $10\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{10}{x}-\sqrt[3]{x})\text{d}x & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{{x}^{4}}+10\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =10(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K)-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{{x}^{4}} \\  & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{{x}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
